name: Basilica of the National Shrine of St. Ann
history: The Passionist order came to West Scranton in 1902 and built a temporary monastery chapel on a hill locals called the Round Woods. Coal-mine subsidence damaged the site, and the present church, designed by Maginnis & Walsh, was dedicated on 2 April 1929. A weekly novena to St. Ann began in November 1924 under the Passionist Fr. John Joseph Endler, and the annual Solemn Novena each July still draws thousands of pilgrims.
arch: A Lombard Romanesque exterior with an arcaded front. Inside, an open timber ceiling with painted trusses runs to a half dome over the altar.
features: A carved wooden statue of St. Ann teaching the young Mary, about ten feet tall, stands in the shrine.
A stone grotto stands outside the church.

look.d: Lombard Romanesque arches by Maginnis & Walsh, the Boston firm also behind the National Shrine in Washington.
An outdoor shrine on the monastery grounds.
In 1913 a mine slide under the grounds stopped; devotees credit St. Ann (tradition).

fun: In 1958 the Solemn Novena was reported to draw more than 400,000 people.
journal: Scranton, coal under the hill. The ground shifted, the people stayed and prayed to St. Ann.
